meta.title: Slips, Trips, and Falls in Construction Environments
meta.description: Covers the causes of slips, trips, and same-level falls on construction sites, including walking surface hazards, housekeeping practices, footwear selection, emergency response, and OSHA construction fall prevention requirements.

slip-trip-fall-intro.title: Introduction to Slips, Trips, and Falls
slip-trip-fall-intro.content: Slips, trips, and falls are among the leading causes of injuries in construction. Same-level falls, where a worker falls on the same floor or ground level rather than from a height, can cause broken bones, back injuries, concussions, and other serious harm. OSHA's 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M establishes fall prevention requirements for construction. Most slips, trips, and falls have identifiable causes that can be recognized and controlled.

balance-momentum.title: Balance, Center of Gravity, and Momentum
balance-momentum.content: The body stays upright by keeping its center of gravity over its base of support. Walking, reaching overhead, leaning forward, twisting, or carrying a load can shift that center of gravity. Momentum also matters: the faster a worker moves or the heavier the load, the harder it is to stop or recover from a misstep. Carrying loads low, close to the body, near waist level helps maintain balance. Workers should never carry loads that block their view of the walking path.

how-slips-trips-happen.title: How Slips and Trips Happen
how-slips-trips-happen.content: A slip occurs when footwear loses friction with the walking surface, often caused by water, oil, mud, sawdust, ice, or smooth surfaces. A trip occurs when a foot catches, strikes, or lands unevenly on an object or surface irregularity, such as a tool, cord, loose board, or protruding nail. Understanding the difference helps workers identify specific hazards to address.

walking-surfaces-traction.title: Walking Surfaces and Traction
walking-surfaces-traction.content: Different surfaces provide different levels of traction. Smooth concrete can become extremely slippery when wet, oily, dusty, or covered with sawdust. Plywood, metal decking, ramps, and unfinished wood each have their own hazards. Workers must evaluate surface conditions before walking across them, especially when weather, materials, or construction activities change conditions throughout the day.

housekeeping-maintenance.title: Housekeeping and Hazard Control
housekeeping-maintenance.content: Good housekeeping is one of the most effective defenses against slips, trips, and falls. Walkways, stairways, ramps, and access routes must be kept clear. Loose nails, screws, scrap material, cords, and debris must be removed promptly. Spills should be cleaned immediately. Temporary floor coverings must be secured so they cannot become loose, curl, or shift. Power cords that must cross walkways should be secured or covered properly and removed as soon as no longer needed.

footwear-selection.title: Footwear Selection and Inspection
footwear-selection.content: Footwear must match the work conditions. Slip-resistant soles with adequate tread provide grip on wet, muddy, or sloped surfaces. Workers should inspect their footwear regularly for worn tread, loose soles, cracked heels, damaged stitching, or embedded objects that reduce traction. Footwear with worn or smooth soles should be replaced before use on site.

emergency-response-falls.title: Responding to Falls and Injuries
emergency-response-falls.content: When a fall occurs, coworkers must respond carefully. A seriously injured person should not be moved unless there is an immediate danger requiring movement, because falls can cause head, neck, back, hip, or internal injuries that may not be immediately obvious. Call emergency help when needed. Provide first aid only if trained and authorized. Keep the injured person still and protected until help arrives. Assess the scene before approaching.

questions.questionText: Same-level falls can cause serious injuries.

options.text: True
False

questions.questionText: Which action helps maintain balance while carrying materials?

options.text: Carrying the load high and away from the body
Carrying the load on one shoulder whenever possible
Carrying the load low, close to the body, and near waist level
Carrying the load while walking backward

questions.questionText: Which condition can make smooth concrete more slippery?

options.text: Water
Sawdust
Oil
All of the above

questions.questionText: What should be done with loose nails, screws, and scrap material in walkways?

options.text: Leave them until the end of the week
Kick them to the side
Pick them up or remove them promptly
Cover them with cardboard only

questions.questionText: A temporary floor covering can create a trip hazard if it is loose, curled, or unsecured.

options.text: True
False

questions.questionText: What should workers do when a power cord must temporarily cross a walkway?

options.text: Ignore it because workers should watch their step
Secure or cover it properly, inspect it, and remove it as soon as possible
Stretch it tightly at ankle height
Hide it under loose scrap material

questions.questionText: Why is footwear inspection important on a construction site?

options.text: Footwear never affects slip hazards
Worn tread, loose soles, or embedded objects can reduce traction
Only supervisors need to inspect footwear
New boots are always slip-proof

questions.questionText: A worker notices mud building up at the entrance to a temporary stairway. What is the best response?

options.text: Step around it and say nothing
Wait for someone else to clean it
Clean or report the hazard before it causes a fall
Cover it with loose plastic

questions.questionText: A worker falls and may have injured their neck or back. What should coworkers do?

options.text: Move the worker immediately into a seated position
Keep the worker still, call for emergency help, and provide first aid only if trained
Give the worker food or water
Pull the worker away without checking the area

questions.questionText: Which OSHA construction standard area is especially relevant to fall hazards in construction?

options.text: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M
29 CFR 1904 only
None; OSHA does not address construction fall hazards

questions.questionText: Which footwear characteristic most directly reduces the risk of slipping on a wet or muddy construction surface?

options.text: Steel-toed boots regardless of sole condition
Slip-resistant soles with adequate tread depth and condition
High boots for ankle support
Lightweight sneakers for agility

questions.questionText: Good housekeeping, including removing debris and cleaning spills, is one of the most effective ways to prevent slips, trips, and falls.

options.text: True
False

questions.questionText: What should a worker do when carrying a load that blocks their view of the walking path?

options.text: Continue and trust other workers to clear the way
Walk faster to get through the hazardous area quickly
Reposition the load, reduce the load size, use mechanical assistance, or get help
Lean forward over the load to see better

1.questionText: Which factor is responsible when a worker's foot slides out from under them on a wet surface?

options.text: Too much traction from the footwear
Insufficient friction between the footwear and the surface
The worker moving too slowly
A properly maintained walking surface

2.questionText: A worker's foot catches on a tool left in a walkway and they nearly fall. What type of hazard caused this?

options.text: A trip hazard caused by an obstruction
A slip hazard from inadequate traction
An electrical hazard
A chemical spill hazard

3.questionText: True or False: Falls that occur at the same level as the walking surface cannot cause serious injuries such as fractures or head trauma.

options.text: True
False

4.questionText: How should loads be positioned when being carried to reduce the risk of losing balance?

options.text: Held high overhead for better visibility of the path
Balanced on one shoulder to free one hand
Kept low, close to the body, near waist height
Carried while walking sideways

5.questionText: A worker walks across a smooth concrete floor covered with wet sawdust. What hazard is present?

options.text: No hazard; concrete is always slip-resistant
A minor inconvenience that requires no action
A trip hazard from the sawdust texture only
A slippery surface due to both moisture and debris reducing traction

6.questionText: A worker sees loose bolts and scrap metal pieces near a construction walkway. What should be done?

options.text: Leave them until the shift ends
Push them to the edge of the path
Pick up or remove the material promptly to keep the path clear
Cover them with a sheet of cardboard

7.questionText: True or False: A floor mat that is loose on one corner and slightly curled poses no trip hazard as long as workers are aware of it.

options.text: True
False

8.questionText: A power cord must cross a main construction walkway and cannot be rerouted. What is the next best step?

options.text: Ignore it and let workers step over it
Secure or cover it properly and remove it as soon as it is no longer needed
Tape it tightly at shin height so it is more visible
Mark it with spray paint and leave it in place

9.questionText: A worker's boot sole is cracked and the tread is worn smooth. Why is this a safety concern?

options.text: Worn soles are only a problem for walking on stairs
Worn or damaged soles reduce traction and increase the likelihood of slipping
Boot appearance does not affect safety
Only supervisors need to check footwear condition

10.questionText: Mud has accumulated at the bottom of a construction ramp over two days. A worker approaches to use the ramp. What should they do?

options.text: Use the ramp carefully and hope for the best
Report it to the next shift supervisor
Address the hazard or report it before someone is injured
Cover the mud with a loose floor mat

11.questionText: After a fall, a coworker is on the ground and cannot move their legs. What should you do first?

options.text: Lift the worker upright to check for injuries
Keep the worker still and call for emergency assistance immediately
Help the worker sit up to improve their breathing
Drag the worker out of the work area to a safer location

12.questionText: Which OSHA standard is most directly linked to fall prevention requirements in construction environments?

options.text: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M
29 CFR 1926.502 only

13.questionText: What footwear characteristic is most important for preventing slips on construction surfaces where water, mud, or oil may be present?

options.text: Bright color for visibility
Slip-resistant soles with adequate tread depth and good condition
Steel toes regardless of sole material
High-top design for ankle support

14.questionText: True or False: Regular housekeeping prevents slips, trips, and falls by keeping walkways free of debris, spills, and loose materials.

options.text: True
False

15.questionText: A worker is carrying a large sheet of drywall that completely blocks their forward view of the path. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Continue walking and rely on other workers to move out of the way
Walk quickly to spend less time with blocked vision
Get help, reposition the load, or use mechanical assistance to maintain a clear line of sight
Lean to one side of the drywall to peek around it
